title: GIFT: Gradient Informed Filtering for Distillation Augmented Reasoning RL
authors: Shijie Li, Yilin Gao, Tieyuan Chen, Yun Luo, Weiyao Lin, Hang Yu
abstract: Training large language models for complex reasoning tasks relies on two complementary signals: sparse, outcome-grounded reinforcement learning (RL) for correctness, and dense, token-level distillation for guidance. However, complementarity in supervision does not guarantee compatibility in optimization; imitation-focused distillation can conflict with the outcome-driven RL objective, and existing hybrids lack a principled resolution. We propose \textbf{GIFT} (\textbf{G}radient-\textbf{I}nformed \textbf{F}il\textbf{T}ering for Distillation-Augmented Reasoning RL), a novel method that directly addresses the allocation problem of which teacher updates to apply. GIFT performs a token-level geometric analysis, decomposing the distillation gradient into a component \textbf{parallel} to the RL gradient, which measures first-order conflict and provides a \textbf{safety} filter, and a component \textbf{orthogonal} to it, which quantifies novel directional guidance and provides a measure of \textbf{value}. This decomposition yields a principled scoring rule to rank token-level guidance. We combine this with a progressive \textbf{coverage annealing} schedule that shrinks the budget of tokens receiving distillation, ensuring that the most conflicting updates are discarded first while the most complementary ones are retained at full strength. This facilitates a smooth transition from dense, geometrically-filtered guidance to a pure, outcome-grounded objective at convergence. Extensive experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks show that GIFT consistently outperforms strong baselines across multiple model scales, achieving relative gains of up to 9.5\% on difficult mathematical reasoning tasks. Code: https://github.com/lilifree/GIFT

infographic.key_insight: GIFT filters token-level distillation using gradient geometry to retain teacher guidance that complements outcome-driven reinforcement learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For reasoning-model training, GIFT offers a principled way to allocate teacher supervision while reducing conflict with the RL objective.
method: Decompose each token’s distillation gradient into components parallel and orthogonal to the RL gradient.
Rank guidance by first-order conflict and novel directional value.

infographic.watch_item: Token-level gradient analysis may add training overhead; the abstract does not quantify its computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: GIFT: Gradient Informed Filtering for Distillation Augmented Reasoning RL

title: RoleFlow: Self-Evolving Multi-Role Agentic Collaboration via Structural Adaptation
authors: Yi Ge, Pan Wang, Xuehao Cui, Zian Zeng, Xu Hu, Heng Huang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their adaptability to evolving task requirements. Although recent approaches enable dynamic orchestration, trajectory-level rewards they apply assign one outcome to each decision, ofen struggling to identify the contributions of individual structural changes. We propose RoleFlow, a self-evolving multi-role agentic system that refines collaboration structures through feedback-driven atomic edits and on-demand role synthesis. To make structural adaptation learnable, we introduce Single-Edit Counterfactual Policy Optimization (SECPO), which evaluates each edit against its no-edit counterpart at the same chain state and assigns targeted credit to edit-specific tokens. Across seven benchmarks spanning four domains, RoleFlow achieves the optimal average performance, surpassing the strongest competitor by 4.7 points. It leads on all three multi-hop QA benchmarks by 3.2-7.5 F1 points and also shows supremacy on mathematical reasoning, web interaction, and code generation. Further analyses demonstrate cross-benchmark transferability, training-data efficiency, and cross-executor generalization.

infographic.key_insight: RoleFlow adapts multi-agent collaboration through atomic structural edits and on-demand role synthesis, learning which changes improve task outcomes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive collaboration could reduce reliance on fixed agent workflows for mathematical reasoning, coding, and web interaction.
method: Refine collaboration structures using feedback-driven atomic edits.
Synthesize new agent roles on demand.

infographic.paper_title: RoleFlow: Self-Evolving Multi-Role Agentic Collaboration via Structural Adaptation

title: Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithms
authors: Geetika, Shivani Singh Chauhan, Gauranshi Gupta, Anant Jain, Kaushik Kalyanaraman, Bapi Chatterjee
abstract: Adversarial sharpness penalty per iteration of a base optimizer, known as sharpness-aware minimization (SAM), is an accepted technique to improve generalization in deep learning. Recently, Muon has emerged as a dominant optimization algorithm for training large language models (LLMs). It achieves lower sample complexity for heavy-tailed gradient updates - a phenomenon common in LLM training. However, sharpness penalties with Muon updates are yet largely unexplored in the literature. Moreover, the behavior of SAM under heavy-tailed noise is unknown both theoretically and empirically. A potential reason for this gap is the additional cost of extra gradient computation per iteration for penalty perturbations in SAM, which becomes prohibitive for LLMs. This paper introduces Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithm (SOMA) to combine a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded perturbation scheme with the Muon algorithm. The key idea is to use stale (purely) stochastic gradient noise for adversarial perturbations. Theoretically, we show that SOMA's sample complexity is invariant to the perturbation direction. We provide explorations and insights into SOMA's robustness to heavy-tailed gradient noise. We extensively explore SOMA's efficacy in (a) mitigating quality degradation due to post-training quantization, and (b) catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning of LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: SOMA combines sharpness-aware minimization with Muon using stale stochastic gradient noise for perturbations, with sample complexity theoretically invariant to perturbation direction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SOMA targets computationally efficient LLM optimization while exploring resilience to post-training quantization and catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning.
method: Combine sharpness-aware perturbations with Muon's orthogonalized momentum updates.
Reuse stale stochastic gradient noise to construct adversarial perturbations.
Analyze sample complexity and robustness under heavy-tailed gradient noise.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive evaluations of quantization-related quality degradation and catastrophic forgetting, but provides no datasets, model sizes, or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Verify actual compute savings and sensitivity to stale-noise perturbations at the intended LLM training scale.
infographic.paper_title: Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithms

title: CoPiT: A conditional Position-induced Transformer for aerodynamic field prediction on unstructured meshes
authors: Junfeng Chen, Yongchen Fan, Zhonghua Qiao, Kailiang Wu
abstract: High-fidelity Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations remain a standard tool for aerodynamic analysis, yet each solve on an unstructured mesh is computationally expensive, making many-query tasks such as design exploration, optimization, and multi-condition evaluation costly. Neural operators provide mesh-flexible surrogates for mapping geometry and operating conditions to flow fields; however, in many existing architectures, global parameters such as the freestream state and design variables are concatenated with pointwise inputs, leaving their influence on intermediate features implicit. This paper proposes CoPiT, a \textbf{Co}nditional \textbf{P}osition-induced \textbf{T}ransformer that builds on the Position-induced Transformer (PiT) as its geometric backbone and injects a global condition vector through multi-stage feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), thereby making parametric modulation explicit while preserving geometry-based attention weights. The model is evaluated on two-dimensional AirfRANS airfoil fields, including scarce-data and extrapolation regimes, and on three-dimensional BlendedNet++ blended-wing-body surfaces. On the AirfRANS full-data test set, CoPiT reduces surface and volume losses by approximately 54\% and 24\% relative to Transolver, respectively, and achieves the lowest overall normalized test MSE among the compared baselines on BlendedNet++. Matched ablations show that FiLM conditioning generally improves upon input concatenation, while the preferred placement is task-dependent. CoPiT thus provides a practical operator-learning surrogate for parametric aerodynamics on unstructured meshes.

infographic.key_insight: CoPiT explicitly modulates aerodynamic field predictions with global operating and design conditions while preserving geometry-based attention on unstructured meshes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a surrogate for costly RANS simulations in repeated aerodynamic design exploration, optimization, and multi-condition evaluation.
method: Use the Position-induced Transformer as a mesh-flexible geometric backbone.
Inject global conditions through multi-stage feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM).
Preserve geometry-based attention weights while conditioning intermediate features.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on 2D AirfRANS and 3D BlendedNet++, CoPiT reduces AirfRANS full-data surface and volume losses by approximately 54% and 24% versus Transolver and achieves the lowest overall normalized test MSE among compared BlendedNet++ baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The preferred FiLM placement is task-dependent, so conditioning stages require validation for each application.
infographic.paper_title: CoPiT: A conditional Position-induced Transformer for aerodynamic field prediction on unstructured meshes

title: Discovery of Singularities in Partial Differential Equations Using Adaptive Numerical Discretizations
authors: Allen Yang, Lucas Amoudruz, Petros Koumoutsakos
abstract: We compute self-similar singularity profiles of partial differential equations (PDEs) using adaptive numerical discretizations based on optimizing a discrete loss (ODIL). The fields are represented in overlapping local Chebyshev patches joined with a mapped asymptotic patch. After factoring out the leading power laws of solution ansatzes, their limiting amplitudes at infinity are determined by the optimization, eliminating domain truncation and prescribed far-field conditions. Adaptive refinement is guided by Chebyshev-coefficient decay, and the nonlinear least-squares problem is solved using automatically differentiated Gauss--Newton iterations with Levenberg--Marquardt damping. The method achieves O(10^{-14})-level accuracy for Burgers profiles, residuals of O(10^{-14}) to O(10^{-10}) for the generalized De Gregorio family, and of O(10^{-8}) in a local region for the two-dimensional Boussinesq equations. These results demonstrate that ODIL can identify singularity profiles for PDEs with high accuracy using adaptive numerical methods, complementing ongoing efforts that rely on artificial intelligence.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive optimization of discretized PDEs can recover highly accurate self-similar singularity profiles without domain truncation or prescribed far-field conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers computational scientists a high-accuracy numerical tool for studying singular behavior that complements AI-based methods.
method: Represent fields with overlapping local Chebyshev patches and a mapped asymptotic patch.
Factor out leading power laws and optimize the limiting amplitudes at infinity.
Refine using Chebyshev-coefficient decay and solve with automatically differentiated Gauss–Newton iterations and Levenberg–Marquardt damping.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports O(10^-14)-level accuracy for Burgers profiles, residuals of O(10^-14) to O(10^-10) for generalized De Gregorio equations, and O(10^-8) residuals locally for 2D Boussinesq equations.
infographic.watch_item: Small numerical residuals do not by themselves prove singularity formation, and the reported Boussinesq residual is local rather than global.
infographic.paper_title: Discovery of Singularities in Partial Differential Equations Using Adaptive Numerical Discretizations

title: Accordion: Elastic-Depth Inference via Fixed-Prefix Layer Looping
authors: Yudong Zhang, Wei Ding, Kaili Zheng, Yuchen Ding, Zhenyu Zhang
abstract: Large language models serve applications with diverse inference budgets, but training and maintaining separate models for each budget incurs substantial costs. Recent Looped Transformers enable flexible inference computation through parameter reuse, but maintaining strong performance across different inference budgets remains an open challenge. We introduce Accordion, a mixture-of-experts-based model that supports five inference budgets through fixed-prefix layer looping. Each budget follows a pre-defined execution path, while the minimum budget retains the unlooped model. Joint pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and optimizes its next-token prediction loss without additional cross-budget consistency objectives. We further preserve these inference budgets through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, where parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrate three domain experts into one model. After 3.6T tokens of pretraining, increasing inference depth improves Accordion-6B-A0.5B's five-category macro-average across 37 tasks by 3.01 percentage points, with the middle budget capturing 89% of this gain using half as many additional layer executions. The final model surpasses each domain expert on its corresponding task-and-budget average, while achieving strong instruction-following performance across all budgets and retaining depth-dependent gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

infographic.key_insight: Accordion lets one mixture-of-experts language model serve five inference budgets by repeatedly executing a fixed prefix of layers, improving performance as inference depth increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A shared model with selectable inference depth can reduce the need to train and maintain separate models for different compute budgets.

infographic.watch_item: Additional layer executions increase inference work, and the abstract does not report measured latency or hardware-specific efficiency.
infographic.paper_title: Accordion: Elastic-Depth Inference via Fixed-Prefix Layer Looping

title: A Transformer-based Approach for Real-time Multi-agent Path Planning with Varying Initial/Final Conditions
authors: Qian Zhang, Shanqing Liu, Jerome Darbon, George Karniadakis
abstract: We address the problem of real-time multi-agent path planning under prescribed initial and final configurations, formulated as a high-dimensional optimal control problem subject to inter-agent collision avoidance and obstacle constraints. Classical solvers based on the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or Pontryagin's maximum principle (PMP) become computationally intractable as the number of agents grows, due to the curse of dimensionality and the non-convexity introduced by interaction constraints. We propose OCFormer, a transformer-based neural network that parameterizes the inverse of a coordinate transformation mapping a simple, analytically tractable latent space, in which agents evolve independently under a decoupled Hamiltonian, to the physical space of the coupled, interacting system. The model is trained by minimizing a physics-informed loss comprising the Hamiltonian ODE residual from the PMP and a boundary matching term, without requiring pre-computed trajectory data. The self-attention mechanism endows OCFormer with permutation equivariance over agents, a structural symmetry that prior symplectic network approaches do not natively enforce. When trained on a distribution of boundary conditions, the amortized OCFormer produces near-optimal trajectories for unseen initial and final configurations in a single forward pass ($\sim$220ms), enabling real-time inference without retraining. We further introduce a lightweight transfer learning framework that adapts a pretrained OCFormer to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds via L-BFGS fine-tuning. Numerical experiments on two- and three-dimensional multi-agent navigation with up to 128 agents demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of the proposed approach.

infographic.key_insight: OCFormer learns a transformer-based mapping from simple, independent latent dynamics to coupled multi-agent trajectories, enabling fast planning across varying start and goal configurations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could accelerate collision-aware robot fleet planning by replacing repeated optimal-control solves with amortized inference.
method: Parameterize a latent-to-physical coordinate map with an agent-permutation-equivariant transformer.
Train without precomputed trajectories using Pontryagin Hamiltonian ODE residuals and boundary-matching loss.

infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 2D and 3D navigation experiments with up to 128 agents, approximately 220 ms inference for unseen boundary conditions, and adaptation in seconds.
infographic.watch_item: Physics-informed training alone does not establish hard collision-avoidance guarantees; safety and runtime require validation under deployment conditions.
infographic.paper_title: A Transformer-based Approach for Real-time Multi-agent Path Planning with Varying Initial/Final Conditions

title: Reinforcement Learning for Global-Local Control of Dynamic Networks with Applications to Systemic Risk
authors: Nils Detering, Florian Grell, Thilo Meyer-Brandis
abstract: We propose a reinforcement learning framework for solving control problems on dynamic networks, where control decisions consist of a combination of graph-level (global) and node-level (local) actions. To exploit the underlying network structure in a policy-gradient algorithm, we introduce a message-passing neural network architecture with separate global and local policy heads. The architecture ensures that the resulting policies satisfy natural permutation symmetries and transparency constraints. Our main theoretical contribution is an analysis of the robustness and regularity properties of the proposed architecture. We derive explicit Lipschitz bounds with respect to both parameter and input perturbations and use these estimates to establish convergence guarantees for a projected policy-gradient algorithm. The resulting constants reveal how architectural choices and graph characteristics influence sensitivity to input perturbations and the convergence behavior of gradient-based optimization methods. As an application, we study the management of systemic risk in financial networks, where a regulator allocates capital interventions across interconnected institutions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed reinforcement learning architecture outperforms standard architectures based on feedforward neural networks while the learned policies fulfill desirable symmetry and transparency constraints. The algorithm scales to large networks and effectively combines global budget decisions with local allocation policies by exploiting the underlying graph structure.

infographic.key_insight: A graph-based reinforcement learning architecture coordinates global and node-level control while preserving permutation symmetries and transparency constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports network-wide resource budgeting and local allocation, with applications to capital interventions in interconnected financial institutions.
method: Use a message-passing neural network with separate global and local policy heads.
Derive explicit Lipschitz bounds for input and parameter perturbations.

infographic.evidence_signal: Financial-network experiments report better performance than feedforward neural-network baselines and scalability to large networks, though the abstract provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Sensitivity and optimization behavior depend on architecture and graph characteristics, so robustness should be checked for each target network.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning for Global-Local Control of Dynamic Networks with Applications to Systemic Risk

title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping
authors: Chengxi Li, Hanlin Wu, Zhicheng Cai, Huan-ang Gao, Wei-Ying Ma, Jingjing Liu
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.

infographic.key_insight: EPIC controls policy drift over generated prefixes rather than individual tokens, using an exact reverse-KL coordinate to construct a prefix-level trust region.
infographic.engineering_relevance: EPIC targets long-response and off-policy LLM reinforcement learning, where token-level clipping can miss accumulated changes in the generated context.
method: Model autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process.
Derive cumulative prefix likelihood ratios as exact importance weights for stepwise policy improvement.
Apply PPO-style prefix clipping using r − 1 − log r, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the prefix-distribution reverse KL.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent gains over standard and sequence-level clipping on mathematical-reasoning benchmarks with an off-policy-trained sparse mixture-of-experts LLM, while remaining competitive with routing-replay alternatives.
infographic.watch_item: Cumulative prefix likelihood ratios may require numerical care for long sequences; the abstract provides no quantitative gains or evidence of generalization beyond the reported setting.
infographic.paper_title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping

title: Contextual Decision Making: Predictive or Generative
authors: L. Jeff Hong, Weihuan Huang, Xinyao Li
abstract: Contextual decision making uses observed covariates to guide decisions under uncertainty. Two natural approaches are predict-then-optimize (PtO), which learns the conditional expected objective, and generate-then-optimize (GtO), which learns conditional uncertainty and optimizes using generated scenarios. We study when each approach is preferable by examining how the choice of learning target affects statistical accuracy and optimization tractability. Although PtO learns a narrower target, our regret bounds show how differences in smoothness can offset GtO's additional dimensional burden. Exploiting smoothness also raises an optimization tradeoff: within the class of nonnegative-weight PtO methods studied, a lower bound limits the gains from additional smoothness, while more flexible methods may introduce signed weights and lose the guarantee of preserving convexity. GtO preserves scenario-wise convexity, but requires learning a richer object and generating scenarios for optimization. Synthetic experiments and a real case study illustrate how these tradeoffs vary with data availability and problem structure. Together with the scope for reusing a model across tasks, our findings provide practical guidance for choosing between the approaches without identifying a universal winner.

infographic.key_insight: Neither predict-then-optimize nor generate-then-optimize universally wins: smoothness, learning complexity, and optimization tractability determine the tradeoff.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choose between learning expected objectives and generating uncertainty scenarios based on data availability, convexity requirements, and opportunities to reuse models across tasks.
method: Compare regret bounds for learning conditional expected objectives versus conditional uncertainty.
Analyze how smoothness offsets the dimensional burden of generative learning.
Establish a lower bound for nonnegative-weight predictive methods and examine convexity tradeoffs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic experiments and a real case study illustrate how performance varies with data availability and problem structure.
infographic.watch_item: Flexible predictive methods may use signed weights and lose convexity guarantees, while generative methods require richer learning targets and scenario generation.
infographic.paper_title: Contextual Decision Making: Predictive or Generative

title: Minimax Rates for imperfect Physics-Informed Regression
authors: Nathan Doumèche
abstract: Physics-informed machine learning incorporates physical knowledge into data-driven models, often through a partial differential equation (PDE) that the target is assumed to satisfy. However, how much this knowledge improves statistical performance remains unclear, especially when the physical model is imperfect. Since satisfying a PDE implies being differentiable, a natural benchmark for physics-informed regression is the best achievable performance when smoothness is the only prior information about the target function. We show that there is a characteristic threshold for the modeling error above which the physical prior cannot improve the convergence rate. The form of this threshold is common to every linear PDE and certain nonlinear PDEs. Below it, the gain depends on the equation type. For classes of elliptic and hyperbolic PDEs with constant coefficients, we establish convergence rates that improve continuously as the modeling error decreases, and prove their minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors. With exact physics, the rates correspond to learning in dimension d-1 rather than d, reflecting the freedom left by unknown boundary or initial data. We also give conditions for computing the estimator with near-linear complexity and show how to tune its hyperparameters without knowing the modeling error.

infographic.key_insight: Imperfect physics improves regression convergence rates only below a modeling-error threshold; with exact physics, studied PDE classes yield rates corresponding to dimension d−1 rather than d.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results clarify when PDE constraints can improve statistical efficiency and give conditions for near-linear estimator computation and tuning without knowing the modeling error.
method: Benchmark physics-informed regression against optimal smoothness-only regression.
Derive a modeling-error threshold for all linear PDEs and certain nonlinear PDEs.

infographic.watch_item: Rate gains depend on PDE type and modeling error, while near-linear computation requires additional conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Minimax Rates for imperfect Physics-Informed Regression

title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements
authors: Xinrui Li, Pawan Sasanka Ammanamanchi, Siddharth Bhat, Rianna Jamdar, Yongxi Lin, Stella Biderman
abstract: Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq

infographic.key_insight: SemantEq tests faithful statement equivalence through allowed transformations, avoiding ordinary logical equivalence that can link unrelated provable statements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Separating proof generation from proof acceptance lets stronger provers improve coverage without weakening checks on autoformalized mathematics.
method: Require transformations in both directions using allowed steps such as logical rearrangement and library-equation rewriting.
Search for admissible equivalence proofs with SemantEq-Eval.

infographic.evidence_signal: On the adjudicated ProofNetVerif test split, SemantEq-Eval achieved 100% precision and 65.6% recall versus BEq+'s 95.8% and 61.8%; under the best prompt, ProofAudit raised recall from 65.4% to 81.1% on 407 equivalent pairs while accepting none of 104 non-equivalent pairs.
infographic.watch_item: Results are benchmark-specific, and faithful reformulations outside the allowed transformation policy may be rejected.
infographic.paper_title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements

title: Covariance-Informed Ensemble Score Filtering: Embedding Localized Covariance Geometry into Score-Based Transport
authors: Siming Liang, Peter Jan van Leeuwen, Hristo G. Chipilski, Zezhong Zhang, Feng Bao, Guannan Zhang
abstract: Background-error covariance models are central to atmospheric data assimilation because they spread partial observational information across space, variables, and dynamically coupled scales. Ensemble and variational methods exploit this covariance geometry efficiently, but their standard analysis formulations are largely built around Gaussian or locally quadratic approximations. Score-based ensemble filtering provides a framework for nonlinear distributional transport, but existing Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) formulations lack an intrinsic covariance-mediated pathway for propagating likelihood information from observed to unobserved state components. We introduce a covariance-informed ensemble score filter (CI-EnSF) that embeds localized forecast-error covariance geometry directly into the forward diffusion and reverse transport. The proposed forward diffusion is covariance-shaped in standardized state space and becomes isotropic under the corresponding control-variable transformation. This covariance structure continuously propagates observational information from observed to unobserved state components throughout the reverse transport analysis trajectory. Experiments with Lorenz-96 and surface quasi-geostrophic (SQG) dynamics show a clear regime dependence. For linear observations, a well-tuned LETKF is more accurate, while CI-EnSF maintains stable cycling and effective covariance-mediated information propagation. Under strongly nonlinear observations and under climatological initialization, CI-EnSF achieves lower analysis error and greater cycling robustness than Gaussian ensemble benchmarks such as the LETKF, with improvements extending across spatial scales in the nonlinear SQG experiment. These results suggest that the principal benefit of CI-EnSF arises from combining nonlinear distributional transport with the mature covariance geometry used in conventional data assimilation.

infographic.key_insight: CI-EnSF embeds localized forecast-error covariance geometry into score-based transport so observations can inform unobserved state components throughout the analysis trajectory.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a route to more robust data assimilation in nonlinear dynamical systems by combining ensemble covariance structure with nonlinear distributional transport.
method: Shape forward diffusion using localized forecast-error covariance in standardized state space.
Use a control-variable transformation that makes the diffusion isotropic.
Carry covariance-mediated observational information through reverse transport.
infographic.evidence_signal: Lorenz-96 and SQG experiments show that a well-tuned LETKF is more accurate for linear observations, while CI-EnSF achieves lower analysis error and greater cycling robustness under strongly nonlinear observations and climatological initialization.

infographic.paper_title: Covariance-Informed Ensemble Score Filtering: Embedding Localized Covariance Geometry into Score-Based Transport

title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks
authors: Takeru Hasegawa, Naoto Mitsume, Shota Deguchi, Mitsuteru Asai, Tetsuya Kanagawa
abstract: Interactions between ultrasound and microbubbles underlie a range of biomedical and industrial applications, yet predicting how the physical parameters of the medium and bubbles govern nonlinear wave propagation remains difficult. This study proposes a parameter estimation framework that combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, describing weakly nonlinear wave propagation in a bubbly liquid, with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The contributions are threefold. First, the PINN reproduces the reference solution of the governing equation in the forward problem, with a near-zero prediction error at the initial time that confirms the initial condition is enforced exactly as intended. Second, prior to inverse estimation, a sensitivity analysis is introduced that quantifies, at both the coefficient and solution levels, how each of eight physical parameters influences the KdVB equation, allowing the expected difficulty of estimating each parameter to be assessed in advance. Third, based on this assessment, single-parameter inverse estimation is performed for seven of the eight parameters using the PINN. Liquid viscosity, bubble initial radius, liquid density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are estimated with errors of 0.8-2.1%, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and the surface tension coefficient cannot be estimated at all, consistent with the sensitivity analysis. These results establish a general framework for identifying and estimating the physical parameters governing nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquids from observed waveform data.

infographic.key_insight: Sensitivity analysis helps anticipate which bubbly-liquid parameters a physics-informed neural network can recover from nonlinear waveforms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could guide parameter identification for ultrasound–microbubble models in biomedical and industrial applications.
method: Model weakly nonlinear wave propagation with a Korteweg–de Vries–Burgers equation.
Assess coefficient- and solution-level sensitivity to eight physical parameters.
Use a physics-informed neural network for forward prediction and single-parameter inverse estimation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The PINN reproduced a reference solution and estimated viscosity, initial bubble radius, density, sound speed, and pressure with 0.8–2.1% errors; the polytropic exponent converged partially, while surface tension could not be estimated.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern single-parameter estimation; joint recovery and robustness to noisy experimental waveforms are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks

title: Empirically Calibrated Differential Games for Simulating Driver Interactions
authors: Amirmohammad Khakpour, Nachuan Li, Pedram Beigi, Yu, Nie
abstract: Game-theoretic models can resolve vehicle interactions without hand-written priority rules, but whether they describe human drivers once calibrated has rarely been tested. This study formulates a general-sum differential game of vehicle interactions at urban intersections, calibrates it to observed driving, and evaluates it on data not used for calibration. Each vehicle minimizes a cost that combines speed tracking, adherence to a map-derived lane route, control effort, gap keeping based on the intelligent driver model, a predictive conflict term, and a contact barrier, while perceiving the other vehicles with a delay. The game is solved with a feedback iterative linear-quadratic algorithm, and ten behavioral parameters per vehicle are calibrated by Bayesian optimization on trajectories recorded at four intersections in Washington, D.C. The calibrated game reproduces the trajectories of 819 vehicles with a mean position error of 1.00 m. When only each vehicle's route is known, as in a simulator, it is the most accurate of the compared models on 96 held-out vehicles (7.42 m), and ten-fold cross-validation shows that it is significantly more accurate than calibrated SUMO (by 3.61 m), an inverse reinforcement learning model (by 0.93 m), and independent and cooperative variants of the same model (by 0.33 and 0.32 m). The solutions, computed in 2.1 s for a typical interaction, are verified approximate equilibria. Finally, the conflict and steering weights, which the data do not identify, can be set from safety and comfort targets; together with a stiffer contact barrier, this removes the collisions that otherwise occur in 43% of tight closed-loop conflicts.

infographic.key_insight: An empirically calibrated differential game models driver interactions more accurately than tested baselines while producing verified approximate equilibria.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports realistic intersection simulation without hand-written priority rules, with safety and comfort parameters adjustable to engineering targets.
method: Model drivers with delayed perception and costs for speed, lane adherence, control effort, gap keeping, conflict, and contact.
Solve the general-sum differential game using feedback iterative linear-quadratic optimization.
Calibrate ten behavioral parameters per vehicle through Bayesian optimization of observed trajectories.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using data from four Washington, D.C., intersections, calibration achieved 1.00 m mean position error for 819 vehicles; route-only prediction achieved 7.42 m on 96 held-out vehicles, with ten-fold cross-validation showing significant gains over tested baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Untuned safety parameters led to collisions in 43% of tight closed-loop conflicts; safety-targeted weights and a stiffer contact barrier eliminated collisions in those tests, not necessarily in broader deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Empirically Calibrated Differential Games for Simulating Driver Interactions

title: MS-TTRL: Breaking the Frequency Conflict in Multiple-Solution Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
authors: Zhixia Zhang, Binqian Xu, Huaiyang Wang, Yikun Ban, Dianbo Liu
abstract: Scientific, engineering, and mathematical reasoning tasks can admit multiple valid solutions, while exhaustive annotation of the full solution set is often prohibitively costly. Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) applies reinforcement learning to unlabeled test instances, offering a label-free approach to multiple-solution reasoning. In this setting, generation frequency serves two opposing objectives: correctness estimation favors frequent outcomes, whereas outcome-level diversity preservation favors less frequent outcomes. We term this tension the \textbf{Frequency Conflict}. To resolve this conflict, we propose MS-TTRL, which obtains frequency-independent correctness estimates through Outcome-Level Self-Verification while reserving generation frequency solely for diversity preservation. Three-State Outcome Cache and the Candidate State support verification reuse across repeated observations and confidence-aware handling of ambiguous outcomes, while Confidence-Gated Inverse Probability Scaling selectively strengthens the learning signals of rare, reliably verified outcomes. Experiments across two benchmarks, four multiple-solution tasks, and three backbone models, each evaluated with five random seeds, show that MS-TTRL improves Recovery Rate by 19.13 percentage points on average over the best-performing label-free baseline and approaches the performance of the supervised IPS-GRPO.

infographic.key_insight: MS-TTRL separates correctness verification from generation frequency, resolving the conflict between favoring common answers and preserving rare valid solutions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For reasoning tasks with multiple valid solutions, MS-TTRL enables test-time adaptation without labeled answers while encouraging broader solution recovery.
method: Use Outcome-Level Self-Verification to estimate correctness independently of generation frequency.
Reuse verification through a Three-State Outcome Cache and handle ambiguous outcomes with a Candidate State.
Apply Confidence-Gated Inverse Probability Scaling to strengthen learning from rare, reliably verified outcomes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two benchmarks, four tasks, three backbone models, and five random seeds per evaluation, MS-TTRL improved Recovery Rate by an average of 19.13 percentage points over the best-performing label-free baseline and approached supervised IPS-GRPO.
infographic.watch_item: Rare-outcome reinforcement depends on reliable self-verification; incorrect confidence estimates could amplify invalid solutions.
infographic.paper_title: MS-TTRL: Breaking the Frequency Conflict in Multiple-Solution Test-Time Reinforcement Learning

title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs
authors: Igor' Kontorovich, Miriam N. Wallach
abstract: A common concern is that using large language models (LLMs) lets students offload mathematical work that tasks are designed to elicit. Yet such claims often rest on outcomes (e.g., submitted solutions), rather than on evidence of students' work with LLMs. We followed 23 first-year linear algebra students as they solved three differently designed homework tasks with LLMs. Drawing on self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments, we interpreted each of 429 prompts as a trace of a regulatory event and compared 59 chatlogs with the problem solutions the students submitted. Prompts formed five structures, casting the LLM mainly as a solver, explainer, or validator. The mix of structures shifted across the tasks, and ten of the 15 students who completed all three tasks changed their dominant structure. Most final submissions stayed close to LLM output, including those that followed exchanges in which students had explained, conjectured, and checked their own ideas. We conclude that an LLM-aided submission is not a trustworthy marker of students' offloading of the mathematical work, and that offloading needs to be examined in each regulatory space and part by part rather than as a whole.

infographic.key_insight: A submission that closely matches LLM output does not reliably reveal how much mathematical thinking a student offloaded.
infographic.engineering_relevance: AI-assisted learning tools should capture students’ questioning, reasoning, and checking processes rather than infer engagement from final-answer similarity alone.
method: Followed first-year linear algebra students using LLMs on three differently designed homework tasks.
Interpreted prompts as traces of regulatory events and compared chatlogs with submitted solutions.
Identified five prompt structures positioning the LLM mainly as solver, explainer, or validator.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study analyzed 429 prompts across 59 chatlogs from 23 students; 10 of the 15 students completing all three tasks changed their dominant prompt structure.
infographic.watch_item: The small, context-specific sample and reliance on chat traces limit generalization and do not fully capture students’ thinking outside the recorded exchanges.
infographic.paper_title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs

title: Adaptive Grid Refinement for Optimal Feedback Control
authors: Alen E. Golpashin, Matthew T. Clark, Bruce A. Conway
abstract: This paper introduces an algorithmic approach for adaptive grid refinement for solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) partial differential equation (PDE) to obtain the optimal feedback control. Traditional grid generation methods often face challenges associated with state-space dimensionality, solution regularity, and large variations in the solution. Whereas fixed grid generation methods may fail to capture the intricate details of the optimal solution, our methodology addresses this challenge by dynamically refining the grid used to solve the HJB equation, thereby optimizing computational resource usage while targeting improved solution accuracy. The reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach presented in this study seeks to reduce the node population while constructing a grid with higher node density in regions with large discretization error.

infographic.key_insight: Reinforcement learning guides adaptive grid refinement for Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations, concentrating nodes where discretization error is large to support optimal feedback control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Error-focused grid refinement could reduce computational demands when computing feedback controllers without uniformly increasing state-space resolution.
method: Solve the HJB PDE on a computational grid.
Use reinforcement learning to guide adaptive grid refinement.
Target fewer total nodes with higher density in high-error regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the approach and intended benefits but reports no benchmarks, quantitative accuracy gains, or node-count reductions.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability with state-space dimension and the computational overhead of RL-guided refinement remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Grid Refinement for Optimal Feedback Control

title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method
authors: Yuhe Wang, Zhu Wang, Min Wang
abstract: Physics-informed machine learning has become a major direction in predictive modeling of fluid dynamics, combining governing physics with learned representations. Yet prevailing formulations neither guarantee that small PDE-residual losses imply small solution errors nor scale effectively with increasing problem size. Here we present the neural basis method (NBM) as a new approach for Navier--Stokes dynamics. NBM is built on a ``representation-then-projection'' principle: fixed neural bases define the representation space, while projection of the governing equations determines the expansion coefficients. The same bases define common coordinates for the parametric solution manifold, recasting operator learning as a parameter-to-coefficient mapping and enabling scalability by removing explicit spatial dependence. For incompressible flow, NBM yields a velocity-only formulation whose residual provides an a posteriori velocity-error estimate, establishing a certified, data-free training objective for coefficient learning. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, generalization, and scalability of NBM, with substantial improvements over baselines.

infographic.key_insight: The neural basis method separates fixed neural representations from physics-based projection, enabling scalable Navier–Stokes solution and operator learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shared basis coordinates turn parametric flow prediction into coefficient prediction without explicit spatial dependence, supporting scalable fluid-model surrogates.
method: Define a representation space using fixed neural basis functions.
Project the governing equations to determine expansion coefficients.
Learn parameter-to-coefficient maps with a velocity-only residual that provides an a posteriori velocity-error estimate.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical analysis and numerical experiments showing improvements over baselines in accuracy, efficiency, generalization, and scalability, but gives no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on new flow regimes may depend on how well the fixed basis spans their solutions; basis-selection details are not provided in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method

title: Group Distributionally Robust Optimization over Decentralized Networks
authors: Haomin Bai, Junyan Sun, Quan Cheng, Yuanyu Wan, Lijun Zhang
abstract: We study group distributionally robust optimization (GDRO) over decentralized networks, where workers collaborate to learn robust models by minimizing the maximum local risk. Existing methods optimize only dual-regularized surrogates and establish guarantees for a globally averaged model that is not available to workers. In this paper, we directly optimize the original GDRO objective and establish guarantees for local models in semi-decentralized (SemiDec) and fully decentralized (Dec) settings. A key difficulty is that applying the primal-dual decomposition from centralized GDRO yields worker-dependent losses whose evaluation requires unavailable cross-worker information. To address this challenge, we develop a novel error decomposition that recasts decentralized GDRO as (i) a decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) problem and a prediction-with-expert-advice problem in SemiDec, and as (ii) two coupled D-OCO problems in Dec, with discrepancy terms capturing inconsistencies among local decisions. By isolating consensus errors in analysis, we develop modular frameworks that support different consensus routines. We then establish the \emph{first} per-worker convergence guarantees for optimizing the original GDRO objective over decentralized networks. Instantiations with accelerated gossip and Choco-gossip achieve an $O(\sqrt{(\log m)/T})$ convergence rate over $T$ update rounds, while experiments demonstrate improved worst-worker performance over baselines.

infographic.key_insight: The paper establishes the first per-worker convergence guarantees for decentralized learning that directly minimizes the original GDRO objective: the maximum local risk.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Networked workers can train locally available robust models without relying on an unavailable globally averaged model.
method: Decompose semi-decentralized GDRO into decentralized online convex optimization and prediction with expert advice.
Decompose fully decentralized GDRO into two coupled decentralized online convex optimization problems.
Isolate consensus errors to support modular communication routines, including accelerated gossip and Choco-gossip.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical instantiations achieve O(sqrt(log(m)/T)) convergence over T update rounds, and experiments report improved worst-worker performance over baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance depends on controlling disagreement among workers; the abstract does not quantify communication costs or experimental gains.
infographic.paper_title: Group Distributionally Robust Optimization over Decentralized Networks
